newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Buthelezi slams ANC, claims innocence.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Buthelezi slams ANC, claims innocence.

text.p: Zulu leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi slammed the human rights record of his African National Congress rivals in testimony to South Africa's "truth commission" on Thursday, but said his own hands were clean.

Buthelezi, who leads the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), delivered a 760-page indictment of Nelson Mandela's ANC and the country's former white rulers to the truth commission on human rights under apartheid.
Responding to questions mainly by deputy chairman Alex Boraine, Buthelezi denied that his party had participated in gun running or orchestrated violence.

The Inkatha submission, including a catalogue of attacks on its members, gave no details of any violence blamed on Inkatha. Instead, it accused the ANC of allowing the murder of 420 IFP leaders since the start of last year alone and about 14,000 of its members in total.
Buthelezi told reporters that the four-hour submission would be Inkatha's only contribution to the search for reconciliation because he did not believe the panel could achieve its goals.
"To come to play marbles and appear before the commission is like treating the deaths of our people with disdain. Our coming here is not a signal that the IFP has decided to participate," he said.
IFP chairman Frank Mdlalose said Inkatha would refuse to return and be cross-examined as other parties have agreed to do, but said the panel could submit written questions.

Mdlalose, who is also premier of KwaZulu-Natal province, scene of most of the fighting with Mandela's ANC, told the commission about ANC plots to assassinate Buthelezi and wipe out Inkatha, saying the war was still being fought.
"Our transformation from apartheid is increasingly being revealed as a seven-day wonder. There is no peace and there is no freedom," he said.
Buthelezi cited the ANC's failure to implement a 1994 pre-election promise to submit differences between the parties to international mediation as the major cause of violence.
"Today, there is no mutual trust between me and Mr Mandela. If we can't reconcile at that level I can't see that there will ever be peace between members of the ANC and the IFP," he said.
Buthelezi, South Africa's interior minister, denied any role in violence that has racked his KwaZulu-Natal province for the past decade, killing around 15,000 people since the mid-1980s.

"I know that IFP members and supporters have been drawn into violence. I say I am sorry to South Africa for this because, although I have not orchestrated one single act of violence...I know that the buck stops right in front of me.
"From my side I wish to say that I am sorry for any hurt that I have caused the ANC leadership," he added.

Buthelezi said his party struggled against apartheid without the support or funding given to Mandela's ANC -- which had taken up arms against white rule -- from groups such as the World Council of Churches, adding:
"As we look around this room, we do not see many friends."

In an apparent reference to Desmond Tutu, the Nobel Peace laureate and Anglican archbishop who was for decades a prominent voice of opposition to apartheid, Buthelezi said South Africa needed apologies from "some of South Africa's more political clergy".
Tutu's statutory commission has been given two years to probe the human rights record of the struggle over apartheid, to pardon perpetrators of abuses and to award compensation.

Deputy President Thabo Mbeki of the ANC and former president F.W. de Klerk of the National Party gave details last month of violations perpetrated by their supporters and apologised for their actions.
But Buthelezi said on Thursday this was not enough.

"I believe that the ANC's national executive must apologize to South Africa purposefully, simply and specifically for the planting of bombs on street corners, in discos, in supermarkets and other public places," he said.
